title: Dominic and the Visitor
premise: Rafael Ishikawa hosts a small-town late-night radio show, and for twenty years the calls have come from listeners who died days earlier—voices Rafael has quietly rationalized away. When an excavation crew unearths a door sealed from the inside beneath the old Harrow farm, the calls stop being gentle and start demanding: something was taken in 1974, and it must be returned before the harvest moon rises. Rafael discovers their own mother was one of four people who buried a child alive that year to stop a plague of grief from spreading through town. In the end, Rafael descends through the door, returns the stolen locket that anchored the child's spirit, and takes its place at the microphone so the dead can finally say goodbye—freeing both the town and themselves.
about_author: Gideon Ashgrove is the pen name of a former overnight radio operator who spent a decade in stations too small for ratings and too old for renovations. They write horror about small towns that keep their secrets on the airwaves.

chapters.title: Dead Air
chapters.summary: POV Rafael. During a routine broadcast, a caller named Marcy thanks Rafael for playing her wedding song—Marcy drowned six days ago. Rafael logs it as a prank, but her hands shake through the sign-off. The beat is denial cracking at the edges; we establish Rafael's twenty-year habit of explaining away the impossible.

chapters.title: The Harrow Lot
chapters.summary: POV Rafael. An excavation crew tearing up the derelict Harrow farm strikes something no blueprint shows: a steel door, bolted shut from the inside. Rafael visits the site after hours, drawn by a compulsion they can't name, and hears knocking in rhythm with their own heartbeat. The emotional beat is dread mixed with recognition—the land knows them.

chapters.title: Requests Line
chapters.summary: POV Rafael. The dead callers grow insistent, all asking variations of the same question: 'Did she ever say sorry?' Rafael digs into station archives and finds a 1974 broadcast log with a two-hour gap, redacted by hand in their mother's writing. The beat is obsession taking root; duty to the truth begins outweighing self-protection.

chapters.title: What Mother Kept
chapters.summary: POV Rafael, with flashback interludes. Rafael confronts their dying mother, who gives them a tarnished locket and only says, 'It was mercy. It was mercy.' That night every phone line at the station rings at once, silent except for breathing. The beat is love against loyalty—Rafael must choose between protecting their mother's memory and the town's living.

chapters.title: Four Names
chapters.summary: POV Rafael and alternating sections from Deputy Okafor, who has noticed Rafael digging through county records. Together they identify the 1974 participants: Rafael's mother, the Harrows, and Pastor Ell, all now dead or vanished. A fifth name is scratched out: a child, Wren. The beat is justice outside the law—no statute can touch what these people did.

chapters.title: The Harvest Moon Rises In Six Days
chapters.summary: POV Rafael. The excavation crew abandons the site after finding handprints on the inside of the door—small ones, dozens, layered like sediment. The dead callers begin broadcasting through car radios, baby monitors, anything with a speaker, repeating 'return what was taken.' The beat is escalation; the town itself becomes complicit witness.

chapters.title: Confession on Frequency
chapters.summary: POV Rafael. Out of options, Rafael goes live and tells the whole town the truth about 1974, reading from the recovered records. Half the listenership turns off; the other half starts arriving at the Harrow lot carrying candles, then shovels. The beat is belonging—Rafael stops being invisible and becomes the voice the town must answer to.

chapters.title: Inside the Door
chapters.summary: POV Rafael, descending alone past the point where the candles' light fails. Behind the door is not a room but the broadcast studio as it stood in 1974, still warm, still humming, with a child-sized chair facing a dead microphone. Wren appears—not monstrous, just waiting. The beat is terror transfigured into terrible tenderness.

chapters.title: Return What Was Taken
chapters.summary: POV Rafael, climax. Wren doesn't want revenge; she wants her name spoken and her locket returned so she can stop being a secret. Rafael speaks her name on air through the dead microphone, which suddenly carries, and places the locket in her hands as the harvest moon crests. The harvest begins anyway—but it takes only what was offered: Rafael's place behind the desk.

chapters.title: Sign-Off
chapters.summary: POV Deputy Okafor, then Rafael's final broadcast. The dead callers make one last round of calls—goodbyes this time—and go quiet forever. Rafael remains at the microphone beyond the door, hosting a show for an audience no living person can hear, content at last to belong somewhere. Okafor keeps the frequency open. The beat is bittersweet resolution: justice rendered, love outlasting duty.
